transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2027-01-05
- Time: 15:00 UTC
- Duration: 01:12
- Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (CISO, Orchid), Markus Hsu (Infra), Priya Nair (Compliance)

Auto Summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
Redwood team walked through private/hybrid deployment security controls focusing on network airlock, egress proxies, KMS/HSM integration, and audit logging retention for SOC 2/ISO. Customer asked about SSO/RBAC mapping, SIEM/forwarding, and data residency constraints. Next steps: share docs and draft architecture, schedule on-prem staging demo.

Topics:
- SOC 2 / ISO scoping and evidence
- RBAC / SSO (Okta, SAML, SCIM) mapping
- Audit logs & SIEM integration (retention, integrity)
- KMS / HSM key flow and rotation
- Network isolation: ingress controls, airlock, egress proxy patterns
- Firewalling / IPSec / mutual TLS between control plane and runtime

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (AE): All right, hi everyone thanks for carving out time. We're excited to walk through the hybrid airlock patterns and how Redwood's private control plane interfaces with on-prem. I uh, quick roll call — say hi?
[00:12] Lena (CISO): Hi, Lena here. Thanks, Jordan. We got Markus and Priya on too.
[00:18] Markus (Infra): Hey, thanks. We've been really focused on limiting egress to a single proxy and ensuring keys never leave our HSMs.
[00:25] Maya (SE): Great, Markus — that's exactly what we'll show. Quick note, my screen is going to be a drawing of the proposed flows, it's rough but should help.
[00:34] Jordan: Cool. Before we jump, a couple quick qual questions — what's your compliance target? SOC 2 Type II now, and are you also looking at ISO?
[00:43] Priya (Compliance): Yes, SOC 2 Type II in scope. We're also starting ISO 27001 scoping, but right now SOC2 drives evidence requirements. We also need to confirm data residency for EU customer subsets.
[00:54] Jordan: Got it. And current auth? Okta with SAML + SCIM?
[00:59] Lena: Correct — Okta for SSO, we use SCIM for provisioning. We want RBAC mapped to AD groups.
[01:06] Maya: That's straightforward — Redwood supports SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning. For private deployments we can map RBAC to your LDAP/AD groups via SCIM sync; we had a couple customers who did role-claim mapping. Quick caveat — sometimes the claim names are slightly different, so expect a mapping step.
[01:25] Markus: Good. On the network side: we're on-prem, segmented DC. We want no direct outbound to public internet from the inference hosts except through an egress proxy under our control. Can Redwood support an outbound-only allowed list/pinned endpoints?
[01:39] Maya: Yes. The typical pattern is an airlock: inference hosts run in an isolated subnet, they only communicate outbound to an egress proxy (could be a proxy fleet or NAT with proxy rules), and that proxy performs TLS termination to Redwood endpoints. We support mutual TLS and certificate pinning so the egress proxy can authenticate to Redwood and vice versa.
[01:58] Markus: When you say mutual TLS, do you expect us to hand over certs or do you manage cert rotation?
[02:05] Jordan: We generally support both. For Private deployments customers hand over a CA chain and we accept leaf certs, or Redwood can integrate with your PKI via a CSR flow. For airgapped setups we can also operate with pre-shared certs.
[02:18] Priya: And keys — we require HSM-backed KMS for any production keys. How does Redwood handle encryption at rest and key rotation for model artifact keys?
[02:28] Maya: Redwood Private can integrate with your external KMS/HSM (AWS CloudHSM, Vault HSM, or on-prem HSM via PKCS#11). The model artifacts are encrypted with envelope encryption: a data key encrypted by the HSM-wrapped master key. We don't persist plaintext keys on disk. Rotation is done by generating a new data key and re-wrapping, we can do rewraps online. Note: in transcription the term is "K-V cash" sometimes — sorry the auto transcript also mangled KV cache earlier.
[02:54] Markus: Good — what about audit logs? We need tamper-evident logs forwarded to our SIEM with 7 year retention for some regs.
[03:03] Jordan: We can stream audit logs (admin events, model-pull, inference request metadata) to your SIEM via syslog/HTTPS forwarder. For tamper evidence we support signed log bundling and optional push to an immutable store (S3 with Object Lock or equivalently your on-prem WORM). Retention policy is configurable per customer.
[03:22] Priya: Do you capture prompt/response content in logs? That's a dealbreaker for PII.
[03:28] Maya: By default we log metadata (request IDs, model version, token counts, latency, failure codes). Content logging is off by default for private deployments; if you enable it we can pipeline it to a customer-controlled storage and apply automatic redaction/tokenization policies. We also have a plugin for automatic PII redaction but you should validate with legal.
[03:47] Lena: Ok. On ISO evidence — we need to know how you handle patching of the runtime, and whether the control plane can be fully in their VPC or do you require outbound to Redwood control plane for model catalog updates?
[04:00] Jordan: Two options: 1) Fully isolated private mode — control plane runs in your VPC (or on-prem) and we ship an appliance; updates are pulled via signed artifacts through your approved egress channel. 2) Hybrid mode — control plane in Redwood managed control plane but we use a short-lived tunnel with mutual auth and can restrict endpoints. For high-regulation customers we recommend option 1 — fully local control plane.
[04:22] Markus: If we do fully local, how do we validate updates? We need signed manifests and reproducible hashes.
[04:27] Maya: We sign all build artifacts; we provide a manifest with SHA256s and an attestations bundle. You can verify before deployment. We also support image scanning and a FIPS mode if you need stricter crypto.
[04:40] Lena: Good. A question on model telemetry: we need to ensure telemetry does not leak customer PII and that any telemetry we allow can be turned off.
[04:50] Maya: Telemetry is configurable. The default telemetry is aggregated metrics (token counts, latency, error rates). Any sample-level telemetry or traces that might include content requires explicit opt-in and will be directed to your storage endpoint.
[05:02] Priya: Ok. Network firewalling — do you have recommendations for egress firewall rules and health-check endpoints? We want the minimal set of CIDRs and ports to open.
[05:12] Maya: We usually recommend opening only 443 to a short list of Redwood egress endpoints or, better yet, only to your internal egress proxy which then has rules. If you use an egress proxy we only need to trust that proxy's cert; ports can be limited to 443 and an internal health port for probes like 8080 if you want internal checks. We'll send a minimal CIDR list, but for private local control plane you could configure it to pull from an internal artifact repo (no external egress).
[05:36] Markus: Can we force all outbound traffic through an egress proxy that performs TLS inspection? We're worried about data exfil via DNS/UDP.
[05:44] Jordan: Yes, most customers place inference hosts in an isolated VLAN and enforce egress via a proxy/NAT and DNS firewall. Redwood itself recommends disabling outbound DNS to public resolvers and using internal resolvers, and we can optionally use mTLS to Harden the session to make TLS inspection unnecessary for the Redwood <-> proxy link.
[06:04] Lena: About SSO/RBAC mapping again: how are service accounts and machine identities handled? We need least privilege for admin consoles and CI.
[06:13] Maya: Service accounts are provisioned via SCIM as machine users, and we support short-lived tokens tied to the KMS for signing requests. For admin UIs we recommend RBAC with granular roles — e.g., infra-admin, model-deploy, audit-reader. We can map those to your AD groups. Token expiration defaults to 1 hour but can be shortened.
[06:36] Priya: For audits, we need a clear chain of custody for who triggered model updates, who pulled which model, and the exact artifact versions.
[06:45] Maya: Our audit logs include user identity (SAML subject), operation, artifact hash, timestamp, and the node that executed the operation. We also store rollout records for canary/rollback events.
[06:59] Markus: On the encryption detail — does the inference runtime keep KV cache data encrypted in memory? We want to avoid long-lived plaintext in RAM if possible.
[07:08] Maya: KV cache is in-process memory for performance; we can enable memory-protection features and scrub on eviction. For extremely sensitive workloads we recommend using dedicated ephemeral nodes per request pattern or encrypting cache values with a data key that is only decrypted within a protected enclave — though that has perf tradeoffs.
[07:32] Jordan: Quick note: there's a tradeoff latency vs cost vs security — some of these mitigations (enclave, per-request decrypt) will add latency. If you want to keep latency tight we recommend the airlock + egress proxy + HSM-wrapped keys pattern as a balanced approach.
[07:50] Lena: Understood. One more on forensic readiness: in event of incident, can we request packet captures or do you provide packet-level telemetry?
[07:58] Maya: We don't retain packet captures by default. We can support ephemeral packet captures for forensics through a gated process; logs and flow records plus application-level tracing are typically sufficient. If you need persistent pcap you must host that capture behind your own controls.
[08:16] Markus: For connectivity between control plane and runtime, do you recommend IPSec tunnels or a VPN?
[08:22] Maya: Both are supported. IPSec site-to-site is common, or you can use TLS-based tunnels for control plane traffic. We recommend mutual TLS with mTLS auth and strict cipher suites if low-latency is desired.
[08:37] Jordan: I know some of you asked about data residency earlier — if a dataset is EU-only how do we ensure it never leaves EU?
[08:44] Maya: If you run Redwood Private in your EU region (control plane + runtime), all data and logs stay inside that deployment. For hybrid with Redwood-managed control plane you'd have to opt into EU-only control plane regions and restrict model artifacts to EU registry. We can add enforcement in the control plane to refuse cross-region model pulls.
[09:04] Priya: Great. Are there any known SOC 2 gaps you typically see with customers doing private deployments?
[09:11] Jordan: Common gaps are around evidence for patching cadence, key rotation proof, and proof of least privilege for service accounts. We provide audit-ready reports for patch windows and key rotation logs, but you'll want to map those to your SOC 2 evidence matrix. We'll share a mapping doc.
[09:29] Lena: Awesome. Let's talk briefly about the proof-of-concept. We'd like a pilot that demonstrates: egress-only airlock, KMS integration with our HSM, and audit forwarding into Splunk. Can Redwood run that in our staging environment?
[09:42] Jordan: Yes — the POC pattern is pretty standard. We'll need a staging subnet, the egress proxy config, credentials for a read-only HSM client or a test key, and a Splunk endpoint for log forwarder. We can do a 2-week POC.
[09:58] Markus: For the staging HSM client, we can provide a test partition. Also, what's the timeline to get the architecture diagram from you?
[10:06] Maya: I can draft an architecture + ACL examples by Tuesday the 12th and include sample iptables/NGINX proxy configs for the egress.
[10:15] Priya: We'll need an evidence checklist for SOC 2 reviewers so they know which artifacts Redwood will provide.
[10:21] Jordan: We'll include a SOC 2 evidence checklist and a mapping to ISO controls. I'll send that with the compliance packet.
[10:28] Speaker 1 (transcript artifact): [crosstalk, inaudible]...
[10:34] Lena: Any blockers on your end for accepting the signed artifact workflow?
[10:38] Markus: No, we just need SHA256 manifests and a way to verify signatures.
[10:42] Maya: Yep, we sign artifacts and provide the manifest. In our hybrid customers we also publish a signing root and revocation list so you can validate.
[10:53] Jordan: Ok, recap and next steps: we'll send SOC2/ISO summary, Maya will draft the hybrid airlock diagram + sample proxy configs, Markus will share internal zoning diagram and egress CIDRs, and we'll schedule the POC/staging demo for the week of Jan 18. Anything else?
[11:12] Lena: Please also include an example RBAC mapping file to show how groups map to Redwood roles.
[11:17] Jordan: Will do.
[11:20] Priya: Also, can you include a sample retention policy for logs and an estimate of storage costs if we keep seven years?
[11:27] Jordan: We'll estimate that in the packet.
[11:30] Markus: Fine. No further technical blockers from infra.
[11:33] Maya: Great — we'll get the diagram and configs out. Thanks everyone.
[11:37] Jordan: Thanks all, speak soon.
